w: What's tested The functional disturbance model: normal function + an event greater than physiologic tolerance gives symptoms What a TMD is (and isn't): a collective term, about half muscle and a third joint, not the same as orofacial pain The five etiologies: mandibular stability, trauma, emotional stress, deep pain input, parafunctional activity Orthopedic vs occlusal stability; orthopedic instability and its risk factors; what the evidence says about occlusion and TMD Occlusal interferences, the "high crown" and protective co-contraction; why prophylactic equilibration isn't supported Occlusal therapy: reversible vs irreversible, splints, the rule of thirds, conservative first Trauma: the five force factors, normal and pathologic mobility, Miller's index; the four mechanisms of wear and the erosion patterns Bruxism: centrally mediated, not started by occlusion, treated by protecting the teeth with a splint 1 Existing interferences: equal in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; prophylactic equilibration not supported A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Existing mediotrusive and laterotrusive contacts are as common in people without symptoms. Don't grind existing interferences to prevent TMD. Introducing an interference can cause problems; removing an old one doesn't help. Existing interferences are another matter. Posterior mediotrusive (non-working) and laterotrusive (working) contacts are equally noted in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients: "that's a very important point." A CO-MIP slide under 2 mm has equal incidence in both groups; over 2 mm, the incidence increases in symptomatic patients; interferences to maximum closure are more common in symptomatic patients. Incidence does not prove causality. Summary. Altering an occlusal contact does influence muscle activity. Introducing an interference can lead to pain or dysfunction. Eliminating existing interferences does not seem to significantly alter the symptoms of TMD. Limited data suggest an interference-free occlusion is associated with a lower incidence of TMD symptoms developing. Current practice: equilibrating a patient's occlusion for prevention is not supported. So when you deliver a crown or a filling, avoid putting in a mediotrusive contact, because that's too sudden a change; but if the patient already had one, taking it away is probably not going to change their symptoms. The precise effect of occlusal stability on symptoms hasn't been established: sometimes related, sometimes not. A better question: does CNS posturing of the mandible anteriorly or anterolaterally to MIP increase risk as a co-factor for muscle and joint disorders? 2 Introducing an interference (the high crown) causes protective co-contraction A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this The high crown: guarded movement to avoid pain, which then makes the muscles sore. The "high" crown. You deliver a crown on #19 that is slightly high (the jaw can feel microns). The patient develops protective muscle co-contraction, a TMD of muscle origin: restricted or guarded mandibular movement from co-contraction of the muscles, as a way to avoid pain from the initial event. There is "nothing pathologic about it": it is a normal, healthy avoidance behavior, and the source can be a high crown, a tooth with an endodontic lesion or a burned palate. But moving in ways we don't normally move leads to generalized muscle soreness and pain (local muscle soreness, myalgia). The conclusion: an unstable occlusal contact influenced muscle activity. Does occlusion cause a specific TMD? In this case, yes. 3 Bruxism is centrally mediated, not started by occlusion; the splint protects the teeth A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this The splint stops bruxism only for a while; its job is to protect the teeth. The primary treatment is a stabilization splint. Placing it gives a temporary cessation of bruxism (a temporary muscle discoordination; in class he said a couple of days to a couple of weeks, the slides say weeks to months), and then the bruxism returns, because it is centrally mediated. So the goal is to brux against the splint and preserve the teeth: "brux against the $400 splint and avoid the $40,000 rehab." There is no cure. Additional recommendations, with little supporting evidence: sleeping on the side, stress management, avoiding alcohol, smoking cessation, hypnosis, acupuncture. 4 What a TMD is: a collective term, muscles ~50%, joints ~35%, not orofacial pain A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this TMD is a collective term: muscles about half, joints about a third, each treated differently. Patients say they "have TMJ," but the TMJ is the joint; the correct term is a temporomandibular disorder (TMD). A TMD is a collective term embracing a number of clinical problems that involve the masticatory muscles, the TMJ, or both. It is not one thing: it is a collection of different clinical entities (over 40), each different, and this has been one of the real problems in how dentistry has tried to treat "TMD patients." What they have in common is that most alter normal function and some, but not always, cause pain of varied severity. 5 Orthopedic instability: ~10% coincident, > 3 mm raises risk, loading (bruxism) adds to it A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Orthopedic instability: 1-2 mm unlikely to matter; over 3 mm raises the risk; loading (bruxism) adds to it. Orthopedic instability: when the teeth are brought into MIP, one (or both) condyles are not in a stable relationship with the disc and fossa. A stable occlusion with unstable joints may lead to an intracapsular disorder (inside the joint capsule; one of the many TMDs, and a common one). Risk factors: the degree of discrepancy (a condylar misposition of 1-2 mm is not likely to create a problem; over 3 mm presents increased risk, and some would say 4 mm); and the amount of loading (patients who brux have greater risk). A greater risk does not mean the patient will have a problem. So in some circumstances occlusion can contribute to a functional disturbance. 6 Conservative first: reversible and irreversible treatments have similar success (50-90%) A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Reversible and irreversible both 50-90%: conservative first. Success. The evidence is weak: a lack of scientific evidence relating therapy to effects (the standard is the double-blind clinical trial), a lack of agreement on TMD diagnostic categories, and some causal factors are hard to control (emotional stress). Long-term success of reversible and irreversible treatments is similar, 50-90%. So the treatment philosophy: because conservative treatment reports similar success, it is the first attempt; non-conservative treatment is attempted if conservative approaches fail. Other factors in the choice: symptoms, condition of the dentition, systemic health, esthetics and finances. A splint is cheap and easy, but a patient can't chew and eat with it all their life. 7 Splints: stabilizing vs repositioning, maxillary vs mandibular, full coverage A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Splints can be maxillary or mandibular, full or partial arch, and stabilizing or repositioning. A stabilizing splint provides occlusal (dental) stability while the joints are seated in an orthopedically stable relationship. A repositioning splint is used in disc displacements, sleep apnea and other cases where a specific non-centric mandibular position is wanted. Many names: occlusal splints, devices or appliances, night guards, anterior bite plates, posterior pivots. 8 The functional disturbance model and the five etiologies Core of the slides · 4 questions in the bank The model: Normal function + Event > Physiologic tolerance ⇒ Symptoms. If normal function plus the event stays below the physiologic tolerance, the patient adapts and has no symptoms; most of the time we tolerate things fairly well. If it exceeds the tolerance, symptoms begin. Each element of the model can change, and an event tolerated on one day may not be tolerable on another. That is the story you hear from TMD patients again and again: fine all their life until last Monday, then on Tuesday intense pain, and you rarely know what changed. There is no sticker on anyone's forehead saying how much they will tolerate. 9 Tooth mobility: 28 µm, 150 µm limit, adapted vs traumatic, Miller's index Core of the slides · 5 questions in the bank Horizontal mobility is always greater than vertical. Single-rooted teeth are more mobile than multi-rooted, and the amount depends on the width of the PDL, the root attachment area, the elasticity of the alveolus and the function (position) of the tooth. A force of about 500 g moves a tooth horizontally 56 to 108 µm; 150 µm is the limit of physiologic horizontal mobility, and beyond it mobility is abnormal or pathologic, an outcome of a functional disturbance. Mobility changes through the day: greatest on arising from sleep, least late in the day after function. Adapted mobility: the tissues adapt or cope and the changes are not progressive; the increased mobility is self-limiting, and a tooth may stay that way for years. Traumatic mobility: the adaptive capacity (biological tolerance) is exceeded, and the mobility increases progressively; this is an indication for splinting the teeth (more surface area to resist the force). To tell them apart you must monitor over time: increasing mobility needs treatment; stable mobility is less of an indication. 10 Mechanisms of wear and the erosion patterns (GERD, bulimia) Core of the slides · 4 questions in the bank Attrition Tooth-to-tooth grinding from normal or parafunctional activity (often bruxism) Facets match and are only at occlusal contacts; shiny with sharp edges; enamel and dentin in the facet at the same height Abrasion "Third-body wear": mechanical raking of a foreign material; habitual Food particles, chewing tobacco; most common is toothbrush-assisted wear Erosion "Chemically assisted wear": acid dissolution, intrinsic (gastric acid) or extrinsic (food and drink acid) Extends beyond the occlusal contacts; dull facets; cupping (dentin wears faster than enamel); "proud restorations" standing above the eroded tooth Abfraction Loss of tooth structure from flexural biomechanical loading (Latin, "to break away") A notch near the CEJ, usually facial; saliva may add "stress corrosion" Erosion patterns. GERD: the classic appearance is erosion on the lingual of all the maxillary teeth to the second molars and the occlusal surfaces of the mandibular molars; often asymmetrical, because in sleep the refluxed acid rolls off the tongue onto the lingual surfaces and patients have a preferred side to sleep on (on the back, both sides). Bulimia nervosa (recurrent binge eating followed by purging, fasting, laxatives, enemas, diuretics or over-exercising): erosion mostly on the maxillary anterior teeth, sometimes to the first premolar, posterior teeth only when long-standing; the maxillary anteriors can be completely destroyed while the mandibular anteriors are not (protected by the tongue and saliva). Carbonated beverage abuse: pattern 1, swish and hold in the vestibule to fizz, then swallow, giving generalized erosion with a satin appearance and islands of exposed dentin; pattern 2, pooling the drink in the back of the mouth to fizz and cool, very severe, with high caries and more wear on the back and front teeth. Citrus fruit abuse: type 1, biting fruit and sucking the juice through the teeth, erodes the front teeth to a "screwdriver" appearance; type 2, biting and chewing on the molars, looks like beverage pooling, with more posterior wear. Less common: drug abuse (aspirin, meth), swimming (chlorinated water, on the side they breathe on) and occupational exposure (battery and galvanizing workers). 11 Muscles vs joints: movement problems in the muscles, loading problems in the joints A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Movement problems: muscles. Pain with the teeth together under load: joints. Example 2: stimulating the masticatory muscles. From EMG studies: if mediotrusive contacts are eliminated, the masseter and temporalis are not activated by a mediotrusive movement. This supports canine guidance. In the classic study (Manns, 1989), a full-coverage maxillary splint was divided into anterior, premolar (intermediate) and molar (posterior) blocks and the EMG recorded with each. Without posterior contact, muscle activity dropped significantly; adding the molar contacts brought it up to full. Two theories came out of it: 1. anterior tooth contact inhibits muscle contraction; 2. a lack of posterior tooth contact fails to activate muscle contraction. Later studies confirmed the second. Posterior contact stimulates the elevator muscles: bite, crunch, close down. That is how we're wired. To sum up occlusion and functional disturbances: acute changes produce protective co-contraction, but most often new engrams develop with little consequence once the interference is resolved. Orthopedic instability must be considerable to matter, and it needs loading forces (such as parafunction) to destabilize. Occlusal problems that weren't a problem before may become one if an event finally exceeds the tolerance, or the tolerance changes: "the straw that broke the camel's back." Two general statements, explored in the TMD course, with exceptions: problems bringing the teeth together (mandibular movement) are often manifested in the muscles; once the teeth are in occlusion, problems with applying force are often manifested in the joints. 12 Abfraction and noncarious cervical lesions: unproven clinically, multifactorial A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Noncarious cervical lesions (NCCLs) are one of the most common demineralization diseases in the body: a cervical defect either smooth, rounded and saucer-like (growing more in height) or a sharp V-shaped notch (growing in height and depth). Caries is often not present but can develop (arrest it with silver diamine fluoride). Prevalence varies in the literature from 10% to 90%, but all accept it increases with age. They are found throughout the mouth, most often on the facial surfaces of maxillary premolars; lingual lesions occur but are rarely severe. Treatment with resin composite is typically delayed until necessary: progression, sensitivity or quality of life, poor esthetics, food collection. The etiology is multifactorial: excessive horizontal toothbrushing, acidic foods and drinks, reflux disease; occlusal factors are associated but not sufficient alone. The concept of abfraction (tensile fatigue flexing the cervical area under occlusal load, separating enamel rods, with saliva inducing "stress corrosion") is supported by in vitro studies, but clinical documentation has neither validated nor rejected it, so it isn't included as a primary mechanism of wear. Clenching, nail biting and a diagnosis of TMD are significantly associated with NCCLs, and the sustained loads of clenching and nail biting are more damaging to mineralized tissue than the dynamic, shifting loads of bruxism. Also flagged in class Occlusal treatment (a splint) can help without occlusion being the cause. The stabilization splint works, but that doesn't make occlusion the cause. Five factors: magnitude, frequency, duration, direction, distribution. Wear patients come in for esthetics, usually late. Abfraction: shown in the lab, not confirmed clinically. Bruxism is centrally mediated (sleep arousal, oxygen saturation, stress, medications, genetics). His closing summary of the lecture.
